contextNote: Chewang Lepcha of Dzongu, popularly known as the ‘Seed Keeper of Dzongu,’ shares traditional knowledge about Lepcha indigenous crops, seed preservation, and cultivation practices learned from his forefathers. He describes nature-based signs, including the appearance and calls of particular birds, used to guide sowing times. contextNote: This is the folklore behind the name of Rey Village in East Sikkim. Dukda Lepcha (Bongthing) recounts that Rey was once full of Calamus plants, which gradually disappeared. In ancient times, villagers believed that evil spirits travelled along a foot trail connecting several settlements in East Sikkim, bringing illness and misfortune. In 1897, under the guidance of Lama Ugen Tenzin Rinpochee, the people of Rey, Mindu and Tingpyam built Rey Lapcho as a sacred protective barrier (Raksha Chakra). Destroyed by an earthquake in 1980, the sacred structure was reconstructed in 2020 under the guidance of Lama Karma Chultim Lepcha, affectionately known as Rey Lama. Today, Rey Lapcho stands as a spiritual guardian of the three villages, symbolizing Lepcha faith, unity, resilience and living cultural heritage.

contextNote: This Lepcha oral narrative recounts the origin of Bish Jharne, a traditional poison healer, through the spiritual transformation of Pande Lhamo under the guidance of Guru Rinpoche. According to the folklore narrated by Dukda Lepcha (Bongthing), Pande Lhamo was once a powerful and fierce hunter who ventured into the hills every evening wearing a garland of bones. Despite her fearsome nature, she maintained profound devotion and respect for Guru Rinpoche, visiting every morning to seek blessings. To test her sincerity, Guru Rinpoche performed a divine Leela by appearing lifeless upon the doorstep. Returning from her hunt, Pande Lhamo refused to step over her Guru's body and instead embraced it in grief, demonstrating unwavering reverence. Moved by her devotion, Guru Rinpoche revealed the spiritual test and bestowed upon her the sacred ability to heal those afflicted by poison, particularly snakebites. From that moment, Pande Lhamo abandoned hunting and became a compassionate protector and healer. The narrative explains that those aspiring to become Bish Jharne practitioners in Sikkim traditionally follow the spiritual teachings associated with Pande Lhamo and Guru Rinpoche, observing dietary restrictions that exclude radish, onion and garlic while maintaining personal purity and disciplined conduct. Pande Lhamo's bone garland is interpreted within this tradition as a symbol of her transformation and triumph over death and poison rather than an emblem of violence. This oral account preserves Lepcha traditional healing beliefs, spiritual ethics, reverence for teachers and the transmission of indigenous knowledge across generations. The healing practices and supernatural events described are presented as elements of oral tradition rather than medically established facts.
